extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal scholars, and practitioners interested in Canadian administrative law and appeals under the CPP/QPP/UI schemes
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical summary of the Pension Appeal Board's (PAB) nature, composition, limits and the scope/procedure of its appellate jurisdiction under the Canada Pension Plan, Quebec Pension Plan and Unemployment Insurance Act. Covers types of decisions appealable, leave requirements, time limits, deference on discretionary powers, referral mechanics, and judicial-review interface.

rubrics_metrics.name: PAB power on CPP contributions appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedies under sections 29 and 30 of the CPP are regarded as 'appeals' in the sense that the PAB's jurisdiction allows it to review challenged decisions in their entirety and to substitute for them its own decisions, at its discretion, either in whole or in part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections 30(1) and 29(2) authorize the PAB 'to decide any question of fact or law necessary to be decided', to determine whether an employee or employer 'may be or is affected thereby', and to 'reverse, affirm or vary' the challenged decision. The scope of questions is exceedingly broad and includes all questions of fact or law required to affirm or reverse the decision under examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of appeal for CPP contributions (no leave required)
rubrics_metrics.description: The appellant's right to have a decision concerning CPP contributions reviewed by the PAB is absolute; no leave of the PAB, its Chairman or any member is required to lodge an appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This absolute right reflects analogy to fiscal levy challenges. The right is, however, subject to a statutory time limit (see separate metric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limit for CPP appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Time limit to lodge appeals (contributions or benefits) is 90 days from the date of transmission of the challenged decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 90-day period may be extended by the PAB (or, since 1975, by one of its members) upon application submitted within the statutory time limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of appealable contribution decisions (section 28)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two types of ministerial decisions are appealable under section 28: a 'determination' by the Minister as to whether any amount should be assessed as payable, and a decision by the Minister 'as to the amount so assessed'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals relating to these determinations implicate questions about inclusion in the plan and the amount assessed; the Minister's determinations are made in the Department of National Revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive test for employment status under CPP
rubrics_metrics.description: The Minister's decision whether a worker's occupation constitutes 'employment' (and thus whether CPP applies) generally depends on (1) whether the occupation is employment remunerated by the employer and (2) whether, assuming salaried employment, it entitles the employee to a pension under section 6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutory definition (s.2(1)) refers implicitly to the common law of work contracts; interpretation of s.6 and regulations under s.7 (excepted employment list) is central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of classification as self-employed
rubrics_metrics.description: If an occupation is characterized as self-employment, appeals contesting CPP application to that occupation fall outside the PAB's jurisdiction and are subject to the fiscal review authorities (Tax Review Board and Federal Court) under section 37.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative amendment of section 37 by regulation could transfer such jurisdiction to the PAB, avoiding potential conflicts between tribunals but losing TRB expertise on self-employed earnings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals to the Minister vs appeals to the PAB (hierarchical v contentious)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeal to the Minister is a hierarchical remedy within the administrative authority (culmination of non-contentious procedure); appeal to the PAB represents contentious review before an external, autonomous body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although both are called 'appeals', their nature and procedures differ substantially — Ministerial appeals are internal reconsiderations, PAB appeals are independent de novo or full reviews (depending on context).

rubrics_metrics.name: PAB power on CPP benefits appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Under sections 85, 86 and 98 of the CPP the PAB can determine 'any question of law or fact as to whether any benefit is payable to a person or the amount of any such benefit', can affirm or vary the challenged decision, and 'take any action in relation thereto that might have been taken by the Review Committee.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since 1977 this includes division between partners of a dissolved marriage of pensionable earnings. The PAB thus has full authority to decide entitlement to CPP benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: PAB's self-declared de novo hearing approach for benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: The PAB has declared its statutory duty 'to hear all issues before us in the widest and most ample way; welcoming, if it be tendered, all new evidence, and proceeding, in general, de novo; so that individual cases receive the fullest consideration.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects the Board's practice of treating benefits appeals as 'new trials' because (a) review committee files are often summary and lack transcripts, and (b) PAB delays may render original facts obsolete — justifying broad fact-finding powers and reception of new evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on PAB review of ministerial discretionary powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The PAB has refused to substitute its own judgment for the Minister's where the Minister has discretionary powers under the Act; it will not replace the Minister's discretion unless the claimant shows the Minister exercised the power in an unreasonable, unjust or arbitrary manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus appellate control is focussed on the manner of exercise of discretion (procedural fairness, reasonableness), not on substituting substantive discretionary outcomes. The PAB may, however, refer matters back to the Minister to allow him to consider information not available earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-reviewability of certain Ministerial extensions (s.84(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: The PAB has declined to review the Minister's exercise of the power under s.84(1) to extend time available to a claimant to appeal a Minister's decision to a Review Committee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an example of a discretionary procedural decision the PAB treats as non-substitutable except for the usual judicial grounds (e.g., unreasonableness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave requirement for benefits appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimant's right of appeal to the PAB in matters of benefits is not absolute; it is subject to leave (permission) by the Chairman or Vice-Chairman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The filtering mechanism is designed to manage workload by rejecting pointless or obviously ill‑founded appeals. The procedure for applying for leave and the criteria used are examined elsewhere in the study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appealable decisions for benefits (Review Committee prerequisite)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions appealable to the PAB in matters of benefits are those handed down by the Review Committees; no decision of the Minister may be directly challenged in an appeal before the PAB under section 83 — the Review Committee must have ruled first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects the two-tier structure: Review Committee (first contentious level) then PAB (second level, subject to leave).

rubrics_metrics.name: PAB jurisdiction over unemployment insurance contributions (s.86)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under section 86 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, the PAB's jurisdiction in unemployment insurance contributions is limited to questions of law connected with the interpretation or application of section 3 (which governs who shall be subject to contributions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By implication the PAB also interprets section 4 and regulations under it. Although restricted to questions of law, the PAB's jurisdiction in this field is quite broad and 'covers, more or less, the entire field' of inclusion/exclusion questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: PAB review powers in UI matters (s.87)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under section 87 the Board possesses full review powers and may substitute its own judgment for the challenged decision, at least with regard to questions of law connected with interpretation or application of section 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The laconic but broad statutory wording supports substitution of judgment in legal questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave requirement and quorum for UI appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of appeal in unemployment-insurance contribution matters is subject to leave of the PAB, collectively given; the Act requires authorization by at least three members (a quorum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes a practical oddity — whereas in analogous jurisdictions leave from the Chairman or Vice-Chairman suffices, here collective leave (three members) is required, though in practice this requirement has been inoperative.

rubrics_metrics.name: No statutory time limit for UI appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Curiously, the Unemployment Insurance Act provides for no time limit for lodging an appeal to the PAB under section 86.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrasts with the 90-day limits in CPP/QPP contexts and is an important procedural distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisions subject to challenge under s.86(1) (Umpire decisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions subject to challenge under section 86(1) are those handed down by the Umpire, the first level of contentious review; the Umpire himself rules on appeals against Ministerial decisions under section 75.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 75 provides three types of Minister decisions analogous to CPP section 28, including determinations of obligation to pay contributions and decisions on reconsideration of assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referral to PAB by the Umpire (s.86(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Referral under section 86(2) is an incident of an appeal to the Umpire whereby the Umpire may refer to the PAB particular legal questions (often those concerning s.3) to be resolved by the PAB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice the referral is used to abbreviate proceedings, avoid conflicts between tribunals, accelerate and consolidate appeals, and promote consistency; referrals may be on the Umpire's initiative or at a party's request.

rubrics_metrics.name: PAB powers on referral analogous to ordinary appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Even though section 87 does not specify powers for cases referred by the Umpire, there is no reason to suppose they differ from ordinary appeals: the PAB may substitute its own judgment for that of the Minister in all questions of law connected with interpretation and application of section 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referral thus effectively enables the PAB to resolve the legal issues that would otherwise provoke parallel litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: QPP appeals and Review Commission powers (section 190+191+192)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 190 of the QPP (Review to Review Commission) and sections 191–192 empower the Commission (PAB) to 'reverse, affirm or vary' a challenged decision and to 'decide any question of fact or of law'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As in the federal plan, the right to appeal is not subject to leave and the time limit is 90 days; the Commission Chairman may extend the period on application within the statutory time limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between internal review and contentious review
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal review (author of the initial decision is requested to modify his own decision) must be clearly differentiated from contentious review (appeal to a distinct or higher authority asked to substitute its own decision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text highlights terminological looseness in QPP s.190's marginal note but insists substantive distinction is important for understanding jurisdiction and procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and institutional character of the PAB
rubrics_metrics.description: The PAB is an autonomous administrative agency exhibiting independence in relations to political authority and specialization in its task; constituted of judges of ordinary courts, it resembles a court of justice but remains an administrative tribunal whose sole function is adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Parliament intended to give the Board a judicial character (members drawn from judges), the PAB is still an administrative tribunal (personae designatae) and is subject to judicial review; its self-definition as a 'judicial tribunal' has affected how it exercises authority (more court-like).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review interface and special exception for the PAB
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative tribunals are subject to review by the courts to ensure they do not exceed jurisdiction and that their procedures are regular; traditionally exercised by provincial superior courts and codified in Federal Court Act sections 18 and 28 for federal tribunals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In 1971 jurisdiction to review federal administrative tribunal decisions was transferred to the Federal Court, but the PAB was expressly excluded from the principal recourse ('application to review and set aside') and is subject only to the recourses set forth under section 18 of the Federal Court Act — a special exception in favour of the PAB.
